title: SerDes Link Model
desc: A high-speed serial link modeled end to end in Python: a lossy channel, TX FFE, a CTLE, a 4-tap DFE, and a closed-loop bang-bang CDR that locks a 200 ppm frequency offset.

detail.body:
September 2026 · SerDes · Mixed-Signal · Personal Research

View the full project, code, and documentation: https://github.com/jackpham-rgb/serdes-link

Stage writeup: https://github.com/jackpham-rgb/serdes-link/blob/main/docs/01-model.md

[SECTION: What this is]

A link model for a 5 Gb/s NRZ serial link, built stage by stage in Python: a differential channel loaded from a Touchstone file, a PRBS15 transmitter with FFE and pulse shaping, a swept continuous-time linear equalizer, a 4-tap sign-sign LMS decision-feedback equalizer, and a closed-loop bang-bang (Alexander) clock-and-data-recovery loop that locks a 200 ppm transmit/receive frequency offset.

Currently running on a synthetic FR4 channel (scikit-rf); a real measured PCB channel is a planned follow-up stage, and drops in with no code changes since the channel loader just takes a file path.

[SECTION: Why I built this]

I wanted a from-scratch, first-principles view of the equalization chain that makes a multi-gigabit link work, rather than treating it as a black box: what a closed eye actually looks like, why a CTLE can overcorrect, what a DFE tap converging to a wrong sign looks like, and why a CDR loop that looks like it's doing something can still be unstable in a way that isn't obvious from a single plot.

[SECTION: What I learned]

Three real bugs shaped this project as much as the working result did: a differential port-numbering convention that silently produced an all-zero transfer function instead of an error, a sign error in the DFE's LMS update that made a single tap diverge instead of converge, and a CDR feedback loop that looked functional but was actually positive feedback, confirmed only by deliberately sweeping the starting phase offset and watching it walk toward the wrong side. Each was caught by a targeted test, not by inspection.

[SECTION: Results]

The raw channel eye at 5 Gb/s over 12 inches of synthetic FR4 is fully closed. CTLE peaking helps up to roughly 8-10 dB and then degrades the eye further past 15 dB. This is a real, measured over-peaking effect, not an assumption. The DFE's dominant tap converges to about -0.48 of the main cursor, and the post-DFE residual still shows four distinct levels rather than two, an honest uncancelled-ISI result rather than a decorative fully-opened eye. The CDR locks a 200 ppm offset with a phase-interpolator correction that ramps linearly to cancel it.

[SECTION: Honesty line]

This is a link model plus a synthetic channel, not a measured board and not a full-rate SerDes PHY tapeout. A measured channel and a SystemVerilog/cocotb version of the DFE and CDR are planned next stages.
detail.status: Stage A (Python link model) complete: channel model, TX, CTLE sweep, DFE, CDR lock, statistical BER. Next: a measured PCB channel.
